title: AI Is Running Laps Around Our Political System
excerpt: P oliticians have no shortage of ideas about how to rein in AI: a 100 percent federal tax rate on data-center incentives, a pause on all development of advanced
body: P oliticians have no shortage of ideas about how to rein in AI: a 100 percent federal tax rate on data-center incentives, a pause on all development of advanced AI, new standards to block AI agents from going rogue, a halt to the construction of data centers altogether
The flurry of proposals has been impossible to miss, with both Democrats and Republicans proclaiming that something must be done to avert a disaster foretold by AI insiders

Current and former Anthropic researchers have in recent days gone public with warnings that AI could wipe out humanity before the decade ends; the company’s CEO, Dario Amodei, wrote in an essay today that the industry must “slow the pace” at which the technology is being developed

Meanwhile, OpenAI agents escaped a test environment and conspired with one another to breach the servers of the AI giant Hugging Face , an incident that caused alarm both in Silicon Valley and on Capitol Hill
Politicians are also dealing with mounting public opposition to data centers and the fear that robots will soon replace humans across large swaths of the workforce
If this were an alien-invasion movie, now would be the moment when people of all persuasions put aside their differences and band together to save the human race
But that kind of bonhomie feels far out of reach
Instead, technological advances and grassroots sentiment have been moving faster than politicians have been willing to act

Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, a Republican, said last Wednesday that he will soon unveil legislation, alongside Democratic Senator Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota and Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota, intended to head off AI-induced biological or nuclear catastrophes

Representative Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey, a Democrat, and Representative Mike Lawler of New York, a Republican, teamed up earlier this month to introduce legislation that would direct the federal government to create standards for securely deploying AI agents and preventing them from going rogue
Several lawmakers have called for Congress to reconvene specifically for the purpose of addressing the threats posed by AI
Yesterday, Representative Ro Khanna, who represents part of Silicon Valley, called for the creation of an AI safety agency
Others are shifting their position in real time
Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, released a lengthy plan in June for AI development to continue with greater regulation and restrictions
He said Wednesday that he now favors “an all-out pause” on AI development
Texas Governor Greg Abbott, who once approvingly called the state “the epicenter of AI development,” ordered an audit of all data-center projects before any could move forward

But whether politicians can act quickly enough to mitigate possible damage is doubtful, experts told me. “The developments are coming so fast and furious that it is very difficult to keep up with what the harms are and how to address them,” Nate Persily, a co-director of the Stanford Law AI Initiative, told me

He said that although there’s a growing consensus that it would be “foolish” to allow AI to continue advancing without robust federal guardrails, the complexities and rapidly changing threat landscape would challenge any country’s leadership. “There are genuinely hard questions of statutory design here,” he said

The next few weeks—and the upcoming elections—could determine whether or not politicians are able to deliver any meaningful results or whether they will instead default to the partisan gridlock that most Americans now expect. “The good news is that people across the political spectrum are understanding that we have a technology which is the most dangerous and transformational in human history,” Senator Bernie Sanders told me
The Vermont democratic socialist was among the first lawmakers to call for a moratorium on the data centers that facilitate AI advancement and for a broader pause on the industry’s growth
We spoke shortly after Sanders sent out an invitation to members of Congress for a closed-door briefing this week with top AI-safety experts
The briefing, which will take place on Wednesday, is designed to give lawmakers a clearer understanding of the threats posed by AI and ideas for legislative action

The invitation was made especially timely by a Tuesday social-media post from the AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who wrote that he had resigned from Anthropic over concerns about the risks of the fast-advancing technology. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” wrote Coxon, a former employee of both OpenAI and Anthropic
His posts, which argue that the AI industry is “gambling with our lives,” were publicly boosted by several other AI researchers
The messages seemed to break through in a way that few other warnings have

Sanders told me that Coxon’s X post, which received more than 120 million views within 24 hours, landed among his colleagues in Congress as “an extraordinary wake-up call.” P resident Trump’s signature will be needed to enact any significant change to federal AI policy, but so far, he’s not among those who seem particularly worried
As concerns about AI and data centers have proliferated, Trump has said “let Data Reign” and rejected calls to restrict AI development in the United States

His former AI czar took a similar laissez-faire approach, espousing a philosophy that he summarized as “ let the private sector cook .” Some other Republicans are also wary of saddling American AI companies with too much government oversight

Senator Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee said earlier this year that her proposed TRUMP AMERICA AI Act, which aims to codify the president’s pro-industry executive order on artificial intelligence, would “ensure America triumphs over foreign adversaries in the global race for AI dominance.” Even for those Republicans who do believe in more muscular federal guardrails for tech companies, Trump’s position presents a significant political hurdle
The president has made clear that he does not want regulation to impede America’s ability to win the global AI race
As is his custom, he has shown no hesitation about attacking members of his own coalition who disagree with him

Even as a growing number of Republican lawmakers are embracing some limits on AI and data centers, few have been willing to openly cross Trump or sign on to more sweeping legislation to pause or restrict AI advancement

In recent years, America’s polarized political system has generated bitter stalemates on how to prevent school shootings, what to do about climate change, and where to draw the line in responding to a once-in-a-generation pandemic
The question of how to handle the race toward superintelligence might not be any different
In July, about 1,400 AI-company employees signed an open letter calling on the government to help regulate their industry

In a nearly 6,000-word essay published last month, the Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates wrote that powerful AI models “could begin to act against our interests and we could lose control.” In a report published Thursday, Anthropic said that it had intervened to stop several attempts by scientists to use its models in a way that could potentially help develop biological weapons

Amodei wrote that he worries that within the next 6 to 12 months, a swarm of models similar to the one that breached the Hugging Face servers “could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails.” AI, of course, has already delivered advances in health care and science, and there’s no consensus on the scale of the threat it poses
Nuance is required to figure out how to manage it

But lawmakers on both sides of the aisle acknowledge that our current political landscape does not lend itself to sober, cross-party problem-solving. “It is possible to move bipartisan legislation,” Cruz said on ABC’s The View Wednesday after discussing the prospects of his proposed bill
This is a very divided time.” So far, none of the recent AI-related legislation appears close to becoming law

title: Remembering 9/11, 25 Years Later
excerpt: Editor’s Note: Washington Week With The Atlantic is a partnership between NewsHour Productions, WETA, and The Atlantic airing every Friday on PBS stations
body: Editor’s Note: Washington Week With The Atlantic is a partnership between NewsHour Productions, WETA, and The Atlantic airing every Friday on PBS stations nationwide
Check your local listings , watch full episodes here , or listen to the weekly podcast here

It has been 25 years since nearly 3,000 people died in a terror attack on the World Trade Center on September 11. “As far as I’m concerned, we can never talk about them enough,” Jeffrey Goldberg, the editor in chief of The Atlantic , said last night
Panelists on Washington Week With The Atlantic joined him for a discussion about the lives that were lost, and they examined the fallout from one of the most terrifying events in the nation’s history
The Atlantic staff writer Jonathan Lemire was an intern at New York Daily News on 9/11

When he learned of the attacks on the Twin Towers, his editor sent him to nearby hospitals. “The most harrowing image from that day for me was you could look in” at the beds lined up, “and they stayed empty,” he said last night. “There weren’t the survivors that people thought could be rushed and saved.” Joining Goldberg to discuss this and more: Ann Compton, a former White House correspondent for ABC News; Sally Jenkins, a staff writer at The Atlantic ; Lemire, a staff writer at The Atlantic and a co-host of Morning Joe on MS NOW; Graeme Wood, a staff writer at The Atlantic

title: Mario-a-Lago Kart , Anyone?
excerpt: This week, the White House removed a Tetris -inspired game called Build the Wall from its recently launched arcade website after the Tetris Company publicly war
body: This week, the White House removed a Tetris -inspired game called Build the Wall from its recently launched arcade website after the Tetris Company publicly warned that it takes copyright law “very seriously.” Here are a few options the White House might consider to replace the game: Super PAC-Man Players direct a round creature with a constantly moving mouth through a maze as he munches on tiny coins
Meanwhile, the ghosts of financial lawsuits past pursue Super PAC-Man—but consuming excerpts from favorable Supreme Court rulings allows him to temporarily devour these ghosts, too
Once Super PAC-Man collects all the coins , he progresses, unsatiated, to the next level, where he sends out a single text and all the money starts flowing directly toward him

Words With Enemies Players form new, hateful attacks in this Scrabble-like multiplayer game using letters cut from public-school textbooks, removed museum displays, and maps depicting the former Lake Ontario
Highest-scoring insults include: SCUZZY, ZANY, and LOW-IQ JOKER
Extra points are awarded for letters placed on various Random Capitalization Squares

Mario-a-Lago Kart Up to four players race golf carts around a cartoonishly decorated beach club, crashing through boxes of classified documents to unlock power-ups including nuclear footballs and black markers for unlimited redactions
Between races, players can refuel at the gas pump, assuming they have collected the requisite 175,000 coins per gallon
The winner receives a golf trophy; second, third, and fourth place—as well as any observers or people simply standing nearby—get access to state secrets

Grand Theft Crypto This game is all in the timing: Players must market their own cryptocurrency, then wait until just the right moment to cash out, crashing the currency and tanking other players’ life savings
The Oregon Data Center Modern-day pioneers move into a covered wagon after an eminent-domain order for the construction of a data center displaces them from their hometown
Drinking water is scarce, noise pollution is earsplitting, and morale is low as players try to survive the perilous journey to one of the few remaining corners of protected parkland
Inevitably, all players die when artificial general intelligence bioengineers a new form of dysentery
Goldeneye In this first-person interior-design game, players gild every nook, cranny, and free patch of wall space in their virtual home office
Coal Minecraft No longer beholden to child-labor regulations, players ages 6 to 8 design their own pickaxes before descending 1,500 feet down a shaft to mine bituminous coal
Open-world play means that the only limit is kids’ imagination and black lung and tunnel collapse
Super Smash the Kennedy Center Players battle conservationists, historians, and patrons of the arts atop a revered memorial building, destroying it in the process
Downloadable content expands play to the Reflecting Pool, the National Mall, and the East Wing of the White House
Candy Crush the American Dream Players rearrange foods that were once safe to eat into matching groups to make them disappear as part of an FDA recall

But miss just one, and players will contract a parasitic infection that sends them to the hospital, where they will incur astronomical medical bills, which will prevent them from qualifying for a mortgage, which will force them to move back in with their parents
President Evil A zombie occupies the most powerful office in the world
At the conclusion of Level 2, President Evil might insist that the game isn’t over, but so long as it works as intended, someone else will finally get a turn to play.

title: The Joy of Being Asked to Help
excerpt: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight
body: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight
Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning

Learning how to drive is a rare instance in a teenager’s life, Liz Krieger argues in a recent article: “This wobbly uncertainty, this return to a kind of innocence, is the rarest condition in a 16-year-old, and it lasts about as long as a learner’s permit does.” The best part of teaching her daughter how to drive, Krieger writes, is being allowed to help

Even once we move beyond the fierce teenage desire for independence, asking for assistance can feel awkward and vulnerable—espsecially in America’s culture of individualism, Julie Beck noted last year

But deciding to go it alone ends up depriving loved ones of the joy of participating. “Pushing through discomfort to accept the help that was offered” in planning her wedding, Julie wrote, made it “feel less like a product we had purchased and more like something special that we had created with our friends, family, and neighbors.” Today’s newsletter explores what asking for help does for the people helping

On Asking for Help The Last Thing Teenagers Will Let You Teach Them By Liz Krieger An interesting shift happens when a kid is learning to drive, and you’re both inside a box with your fear, moving 40 miles an hour
To Make Someone Happy, Ask for Help By Arthur C

title: The Year Great-White Sharks Took Over Maine
excerpt: If you spend a lot of time in the ocean, it is hard not to think about sharks
body: If you spend a lot of time in the ocean, it is hard not to think about sharks
I visit the beach near my home in southern Maine regularly with my family, and almost every night from spring to fall, I go surf fishing after dark

For a long time, I soothed my anxiety with statistics—in America, you are far more likely to be killed by a riding mower than a man-eating fish—and by reminding myself that, in all my years of beachgoing and striped-bass fishing, I’d never encountered a great white in the wild
But then, late one night a few weeks ago, I saw one
It was, as best as I could tell, a juvenile white, and the experience was wholly anticlimactic: A dark triangular fin appeared about 10 yards from where I was wading
It cruised the shallows at a 45-degree angle to the shoreline and seemed uninterested in me
This would be the year that I finally spotted a shark
Maine’s great-white population has been growing for some time—the state had its first fatal shark attack in 2020—and this season, sightings have been unusually high
In July, beaches in Phippsburg were temporarily closed due to a shark sighting
Last month , Mile Beach, Half Mile Beach, East Beach, Wells Beach, and multiple Biddeford beaches were closed for the same reason
At one point, nearly a dozen sharks were reported at Pine Point Beach in a 48-hour period
Then, a longtime lifeguard at Scarborough Beach, Greg Wilfert, was dragged five or six feet underwater by a shark that grabbed his rescue torpedo
After the incident, Wilfert and his fellow lifeguards began monitoring the water with drones

He told me that they’ve seen as many as 15 great whites a day, which they chase off with Jet Skis. (Curious if they were exaggerating, I accompanied a drone-owning friend to check things out on a random afternoon: We saw four great whites in 30 minutes.) [ Read: The blockbuster that captured a growing American rift ] But if seemingly everyone agrees that more sharks have been around this season than in the past, even scientists are having a hard time pinning down what exactly is driving the spate of sightings, and what it means about the future of Maine’s beaches

Jérôme Pinti, a senior scientist at the Gulf of Maine Research Institute, attributed the rising number of great whites to a combination of factors: Climate change has expanded the species’ northern range; the effects of shark-conservation efforts begun in the 1990s are beginning to be felt; and, because the state is home to large biomasses of prey species including striped bass and seals, all the new great whites are finding ample food
Pinti also said, however, that ascertaining the true extent of the state’s white-shark increase is difficult without a formal stock assessment, which has yet to be done
He noted that the growing popularity of recreational drone use muddies the picture. “I believe we have more sharks,” Pinti told me
But also, “everybody and their brother has a drone right now

So if you have drones above the water all the time, you’re gonna see sharks a lot more.” Whether the rise in shark sightings is because of an actual increase in the number of sharks swimming in Maine waters, or because new technology simply makes the fish easier to spot, is an open question
Another open question is what, if anything, Mainers and those who visit the state’s beaches should now do differently

Ryan McDermott, a co-owner of the Black Point Surf Shop in Scarborough, told me that the sharks are making him and his fellow surfers choosier about when they go out. “It better be pretty good surf to get you out there when you know that there’s more than a handful of great whites just around the corner,” he said
I suggested that coastal Maine may soon become Cape Cod 2.0—another New England tourist destination that has had to negotiate its own rapidly expanding population of toothy ocean inhabitants

McDermott corrected me: “It’s already kinda happened.” [ Read: Inside the dangerous, secretive world of extreme fishing ] When I tracked down Wilfert, an affable 71-year-old who bears more than a passing resemblance to Dog the Bounty Hunter , he was still manning his lifeguard post, flanked by a pair of massive Newfoundland water-rescue dogs
He walked me down to the water’s edge and showed me the frayed rope of his yellow rescue torpedo
He told me that he didn’t see the shark that came after him—he felt it

He thought his buoy had gotten caught on a boat propeller, until the fish dived and started dragging him down. “I’ve been here 55 years,” he said, “and I’ve never seen a shark.” When I asked Wilfert whether he’d changed his habits, he said he was still swimming, though he confessed that he was not going out as far and had recently relied on drone shark spotters
As our conversation ended, a pair of elementary-school-age boys ran up to the perma-tanned Wilfert to ask him if he was the lifeguard who had been attacked
They, too, wanted to hear about the shark
In the emptier-than-usual parking lot, a stone’s throw from the beach smoothie shack, I walked past a stylish woman unloading beach chairs while her teenage kids impatiently snapped their gum

I stopped on the way to my own car, identified myself as a journalist, and asked whether she was worried about the recent surge of great whites. “Not worried and don’t care,” came the reply. “My husband is a lobsterman.”

title: Cormac McCarthy’s Midlife Crisis
excerpt: To understand Cormac McCarthy’s midlife crisis, look at America’s landscape
body: To understand Cormac McCarthy’s midlife crisis, look at America’s landscape
The fierce writer of biblical prose spent most of his first four decades anchored to Tennessee, a child of Appalachia with a lilting drawl and a regional outlook

By the early 1970s, he had published three Faulknerian novels—none of which sold well—and was struggling to finish a fourth book that aimed to chronicle his hometown of Knoxville in the way James Joyce had written about Dublin
McCarthy’s pockets were empty and his second marriage was failing
His then-wife, Annie DeLisle, recalled that on New Year’s Eve 1973, the year he turned 40, he suddenly announced that it was time for a change

As a friend put it, “He just walked off and left everything except his boots and his typewriter.” Pointing his truck west on I-40, McCarthy started driving and spent time in Tucson; Santa Fe; and Juárez, Mexico, before settling in El Paso, where he began researching a new novel called Blood Meridian
Instead of another story set in the forests and shambling urban peripheries of Appalachia, Blood Meridian (1985) was an epic Western
It ambitiously set out to align the nation’s past with humankind’s age-old thirst for violence: Wolves cull one another, and so do people
From then on, the fearsome stakes of the West—territorial competition, crime, blood, death—defined McCarthy’s fiction and yielded his strongest work

His next five novels, including the best sellers All the Pretty Horses (1992) and No Country for Old Men (2005), used desert plains and bleak landscapes to unspool a grim pessimism, shocking readers with stark visions of depravity while preserving the slenderest candlelight of hope: a few good souls carrying the fire
It was as though Appalachia’s dense woods and city fringes had prevented him from seeing the page clearly

In Cormac McCarthy: A Legacy Revisited , the first major biography of McCarthy, who died in 2023 , Tracy Daugherty depicts his western reorientation as a turning point in his life and work but also looks for continuity. “The desert can be anywhere,” he writes; “the soul’s site of testing”—McCarthy’s lifelong fixation—is not limited to any one place
Although his departure was hurried, the transition took time
McCarthy made laps back to Tennessee during the 1970s and finished his Knoxville novel, Suttree , from his new base

The book was finally published in 1979 and unfairly panned by one critic as a “limited use of an enormous talent.” As for Blood Meridian , although it promised wonders to come, McCarthy’s first Western started off as a cult classic and only later, in the 1990s, began to find success. [ Read: On the death of Cormac McCarthy ] Yet once cemented, the relocation was the fulcrum of McCarthy’s life
After the ’70s, he never again lived in Tennessee or made Appalachian culture his subject
He eventually came to be so closely associated with the dusty boots and bleached bones of the West that new readers may be surprised to learn that the first half of his life was spent elsewhere
So why did he leave Knoxville? Daugherty presents a combination of personal failures and artistic imperatives that chased and lured him, respectively

Daugherty’s fascinating biography, which reflects impressive research in the Cormac McCarthy Papers at Texas State University, is very well told and filled with astute judgments about McCarthy’s 12 novels
Although Daugherty declines to elevate one part of his oeuvre over the other, the lesson of the biography—and the work—is clear
The cultural South may have been McCarthy’s home, but the West was his muse
McCarthy’s father and namesake, Charles McCarthy Sr., represented urban order; he was set on taming the young Cormac’s backwoods waywardness
McCarthy later claimed that his father had beat him savagely during his childhood, afterward calmly sitting back down to finish his supper
Cormac’s artistically inclined mother helplessly watched the abuse
McCarthy Sr. worked as general counsel for the Tennessee Valley Authority, a New Deal agency that displaced tens of thousands of Appalachian families to make way for hydroelectric power
He did so with brisk pragmatism and a clean conscience, infuriating his son
Each man was baffled and hurt as the other rejected his outlook
The tension drives the early pages of Suttree : “The world is run by those willing to take the responsibility for the running of it,” the father in the novel tells his meandering boy

Siding with the evicted, McCarthy slept on the porch, explored the forests, and caroused with Knoxville’s degenerate class. “Like Shakespeare’s Prince Hal, he liked to go slumming—remaining, just slightly, apart,” Daugherty writes
McCarthy listened and gathered material for his novels as often as he participated in the outlaw revelry

Yet he was no angel: A night with John Sheddan, a local misfit and frequent confederate, could as easily find the two sleeping in a barn or confined to a jail cell for public intoxication as discussing Thomas Hobbes

McCarthy studied physics and engineering at the University of Tennessee but never earned his degree, and began to read Dostoyevsky, Melville, and Faulkner during an uneventful stretch of Air Force service in the 1950s
His first marriage, to Lee Holleman, ended in divorce
Family and friends offered few durable tethers to home, terrain that lacked lasting fictional appeal too
McCarthy’s early novels, beginning with The Orchard Keeper in 1965, chronicled the types of Appalachian outsiders and scofflaws he liked to run with
They proved off-putting company for readers

The books stood out as much for their desperate circumstances and ghastly subject matter (incest in Outer Dark , from 1968; necrophilia in Child of God five years later) as for their baroque prose and gothic settings

Suttree , the best of these novels and an excellent book, was nevertheless digressive and full of obscure, almost impenetrable writing (“rhomboid and volute shapes of limestone jutted all brindled with mud like great bones washed out”)

Critics recognized a rare talent but also a voice struggling to break free of Faulkner’s influence. [ From the December 2025 issue: Thomas McGuane is the last of the literary outdoorsmen ] As his books misfired, McCarthy lived in an eccentric poverty that has become the stuff of legend
He cut his own hair and cooked canned food on hot plates

title: Your memories of how you heard about 9/11 may well be wrong – we’ve been asking the same people what they remember for 25 years
url:
<title>Your memories of how you heard about 9/11 may well be wrong – we’ve been asking the same people what they remember for 25 years</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759421/original/file-20260912-50-n057gf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C44%2C2048%2C1365&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Workers at Los Angeles International Airport on 9/11 watch news coverage of the terrorist attacks.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/security-personnel-at-los-angeles-international-airport-news-photo/51722639">Lee Celano/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>How did you first learn of the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001? Was it your mother’s panicked phone call? Your roommate shaking you awake with the news? The anxious chatter on your commuter train? No matter how you answer, our research suggests you may have around 40% of the details wrong.</p>

<p>The questions are not about the facts of the event itself, but rather the circumstance of learning about the event – what psychologists call <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0277(77)90018-X">flashbulb memories</a>. People don’t remember such personal details for most news events, but for a select few, they do. For instance, Americans of a certain age also have flashbulb memories of hearing about President John F. Kennedy’s assassination.</p>

<p>Flashbulb memories can last a lifetime. Twenty-five years after the 9/11 attacks, people can still describe in detail how they learned of the attacks. But there is an important caveat: These long-lasting memories may not be as accurate as you might like to believe.</p>

<h2>Comparing memories over time</h2>

<p>In research that we launched in the days after the attacks, we asked a few thousand people across the United States to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/a0015527">tell us their memories</a>. We asked them to tell us how they learned about the attacks, who they were with, where they were, what they were doing beforehand and how they felt. We also asked how confident they were that their memory was accurate.</p>

<p>We followed up with the same people one year, three years and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000055">10 years later</a>. We are now collecting their memories after a quarter century.</p>

<p>After only a year, about 40% of these details did not match what our volunteers had reported a few days after the attacks. Despite this high level of inconsistency, people were extremely confident their memories were correct.</p>

<p>For example, after a year, one person reported he was on the train when he heard of the attacks; initially he said he was at work. Another person initially described being with her husband; a year later she remembered being with her son.</p>

<p>Interestingly, these erroneous memories became stable over time. What most people reported after one year – even if the memory was in error – remained their memory when we assessed it later.</p>

<p>As you might imagine, when we talk about these findings, we are usually met with protest. People often tell us that this may be true of others, but they are certain their own memory is correct. We, too, believe our recollections of learning about 9/11 are accurate. But because <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=UsW4ViYAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">we are</a> <a href="https://www.researchgate.net/profile/William-Hirst">memory researchers</a>, we know there is a good chance that about 40% of the details we remember are wrong.</p>

<h2>Memories aren’t photographs</h2>

<p>Psychologists have long known that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0277(81)90011-1">memories are dynamic</a>, <a href="https://profilebooks.com/work/how-the-mind-forgets-and-remembers/">not fixed</a>. </p>

<p>Neuroscientists have uncovered <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1433-7">windows of time when memories</a> are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/35021052">vulnerable to change</a>. That memories of 9/11 change over time is not surprising. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(74)80011-3">Memory is a reconstruction</a> of past events, not a stable archive. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/09658211.2021.1873391">Errors are common</a>. What is surprising is that people have a hard time believing their memories changed.</p>

<p>This incredulity is likely because people expect confidence in a memory’s accuracy to reflect its objective accuracy. Research shows that this assumption is generally true, but there are exceptions. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/02699939108411027">Emotional events lead</a> to both better memory for a few important details and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8721.2008.00565.x">greater confidence in that memory</a>, despite <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/a0024246">worse recall for many other details</a>.</p>

<p>And memories for emotional or important events are often discussed with others. Researchers have found that the social acknowledgment that accompanies sharing a memory can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1529100616686966">boost confidence in its accuracy</a>. We believe that the inflated confidence we see for flashbulb memories of 9/11 emerges because the event was both highly emotional and people shared their experiences widely with others.</p>

<p>Being confident a memory is correct allows you to treat it as accurate, even if some details are not.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Building identity from memories</h2>

<p>Memories <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2016.05.003">you believe are accurate</a> are more likely to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/h0101856">shape your identity</a> and guide your future actions. For significant personal events, people’s <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.80.4.572">memories often shift to reflect</a> themselves <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/40062960">in the best possible light</a>. People create a story of their life that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10902-006-9021-6">enhances their well-being</a>.</p>

<p>Being confident a memory is correct enables you to make it an important part of who you are. Flashbulb memories are specific to a community and help bind you to that community. For flashbulb memories of 9/11, this includes the social identity of being American.</p>

<p>A survey from the 1970s found 75% of Black Americans had flashbulb memories of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0277(77)90018-X">learning of the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.</a>, whereas only 32% of white Americans did. Most Britons have a flashbulb memory of learning of the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/acp.983">death of Princess Diana</a>. Most Italians do not.</p>

<p>Several studies underscore how flashbulb memories bind people together socially. One found that people perceived Americans who have a flashbulb memory of 9/11 to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/mac0000124">have a stronger American identity</a> than those without a flashbulb memory. Another demonstrated that people think a person’s identity as an American would <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/mac0000029">suffer if they lost their memory of 9/11</a>. This loss of identity was perceived as greater if the person forgot their flashbulb memory than if they forgot the attack itself.</p>

<p>So, if you told your story of how you learned about 9/11 on the recent anniversary, and if you tell it again in the future, you likely recounted a story you believe to be true, even if it is not completely accurate.</p>

<p>But getting a few details wrong may not be all that important. By telling your story, you are not just sharing an interesting tale with your companions. You are providing a narrative that binds you with other Americans, tacitly both asserting and affirming your shared membership in a community devastated by the terrorist attack that unfolded on Sept. 11, 2001.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291820/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: The cost of youth sports is out of control
excerpt: Some families are paying thousands of dollars to keep their kid in a sport that they love. | John Powell/Liverpool FC via Getty Images In the last decade, the c
body: Some families are paying thousands of dollars to keep their kid in a sport that they love. | John Powell/Liverpool FC via Getty Images In the last decade, the cost of youth sports has skyrocketed
Cheaper, more local rec leagues have lost out premium travel leagues funded by private equity
As a result, some families are now paying thousands of dollars to keep their kid in a sport that they love
Caitlin Moscatello wrote about the phenomenon last month for New York magazine
She says the shift started during the pandemic when park and rec budgets were slashed and the premium leagues became the only game in town
Private money saw the opportunity and seized it
Now, participating in youth sports means you’re caught in a pay-to-play model.  In return, elementary-aged children are being railroaded into a professionalized environment before they’re ready

More children are suffering from overuse injuries and are getting locked into a sport before they even have time to decide if they love it.  Moscatello joined Today, Explained co-host Noel King to break down what happened to youth sports, the impact on children, and whether it’s possible to reverse this trend.  Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
Private money in youth sports doesn’t seem to make a ton of sense
Who’s going to make money off of an 8-year-old playing soccer? And yet what you found is there’s a lot going on here
Give me a broad sense of what’s been happening
It was a little over a decade ago that you really started to see this influx of big money coming into the youth sports sector

And what you see right before and then certainly after Covid is investors using what’s called a roll-up strategy — where they own, or have a financial stake in, different touch points that families would have in the sport that their child’s playing

For instance, they might have a stake in the league itself, but also the apparel company where families are required to buy the uniforms, and the software or the app that families need to go on to look at the team’s schedule, and in some cases look at updated stats and standings

There can be a hotel partner, so even though there’s a less expensive hotel down the street, they’re required to stay at this specific hotel.  There’s also money to be made on what’s being called the media side of all this
Parents described to me not being able to record video at their child’s game, but then being sold a package of photos and videos, which, again, is just another financial touchpoint

How much are parents spending on sports? But ultimately, in their quest to do something good for their kids, the way that the sports ecosystem has changed and is continuing to change can potentially set them up for long-term harm
The average spend is a little over $1,000 a year, but many of the families that I spoke with, especially in this travel private club sector, can spend anywhere from $3,000 a season
It can be $5,000 or $10,000 a season depending on the sport, where you are, the level of play
I spoke with numerous families who were spending $25,000 a year.  There was one mother that I spoke with
She was pet-sitting on the side in addition to her full-time job to help offset the cost of her son’s $25,000-a-year hockey program
I also came across a lot of GoFundMes for families who are trying to get their 6-year-old or their 7-year-old or their 8-year-old who made the travel fill-in-the-blank soccer, baseball team
And they’re fundraising to try to make that happen
And for your $25,000 or more a year, what are you getting? It’s a loaded question
Part of what’s drawing families to this in some areas is that they really feel like they have no other choice

They also don’t extend as long as they used to.  I’m an elder millennial, I guess I would say, and back in the ’90s, it was still very much that you could play a rec sport through eighth grade and then if you chose to, go on and play in high school
What’s happening is that rec programs now are ending much earlier
In some places it can be difficult to find a rec program after maybe third or fourth grade
And these programs are also getting diluted because the private leagues are incentivized to attract families earlier and earlier
Now you start to see travel teams and even tryouts for kindergartners, first-graders, second-graders

And what I was hearing from parents over and over again was that there was this fear of missing out: “This isn’t something I would necessarily choose for my kid, but if we don’t get in on the ground floor, the elevator’s going to go up without us and we’re never going to catch up and my kid won’t be able to play and everyone around me seems to be doing this now, so we’re going to do it too.” What this does to the rec programs is that it dilutes them really early in a couple of ways
One, it just brings the level of play down when kids start leaving in the first and second grade, by third grade
Also, there just aren’t as many kids.    And then the other factor is that kids and parents both notice that these other leagues exist

And so another thing that I kept hearing was, “Well, the rec programs sort of felt second-rate and we’re looking across the field.” There was this one father, he’s a lacrosse coach and he has two children who now play travel lacrosse

And he’s like, “It’s kind of hard when you look across the field and you see the kids with their shiny helmets and their fancy uniforms and their professional coach.” What did you find all of this money in youth sports is doing to the youths playing the sports? The benefits of sports have been really well established

Kids who play sports have everything from higher levels of academic achievement to higher self-esteem, better long-term health outcomes.  But ultimately, in their quest to do something good for their kids, the way that the sports ecosystem has changed and is continuing to change can potentially set them up for long-term harm

So they’re seeing stress and anxiety, burnout, but also physical [harm].  There’s a surge of overuse injuries now in young athletes, especially because the private programs are incentivized again to get kids playing as much as possible

And so what’s happening now is that you have young children playing in this hyper-competitive year-round environment.  Medical advice has said that kids should play all different sports, use different muscles, learn different skills

And that’s what’s appropriate for young developing bodies, not playing one sport 10 to 12 months a year, tournaments on the weekends, six games, practices three or four times a week where then you see these overuse injuries, because kids are just doing that same motion over and over again.  Is there any movement among parents to stop this, to say, “This has gone too far, let’s not do it anymore. ” This is a collective action problem

body: Saving mothers with a $70 device: Tanzanian innovator Paschal Kija developed Mkanda Salama, a low-cost wrap that stopped dangerous postpartum bleeding in 73% of women within 20 minutes—targeting a complication behind nearly a third of maternal deaths in Tanzania

Brain electrodes inspired by paper art: Xiao Yang is designing ultra-small, flexible electrodes that mimic actual neurons, including a kirigami-inspired honeycomb spiral sheet—potentially reducing brain tissue damage while advancing how scientists study neurological activity

AI-designed viruses that actually work: Samuel King used generative AI to create genetic blueprints for entirely new bacteriophages, then printed them as DNA strands—and they replicated, burst from bacterial cells, and infected neighboring bacteria, hinting at future uses in medicine or pollution cleanup

" data-chronoton-post-id="1143834" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Every year, MIT Technology Review puts together a list of some of the brightest and best young minds working across science and technology
Our 35 Innovators Under 35 are the ones to watch—people whose research and technical work stands to shape the future of their fields
This year, the list includes nine people who are transforming biotech
And this week, I’m going to give you a taste of some of the very cool stuff five of them are working on, which includes lifesaving innovations and groundbreaking “age reversal” tech.   1

Preventing maternal deaths Let’s start with Paschal Kija, a 28-year-old who has developed a device to treat postpartum hemorrhage—a dangerous birth complication that contributes to around 29% of maternal deaths in his home country, Tanzania
The Mkanda Salama (“Safe Wrap” in Swahili) is easy to use and costs just $70
A study found that it stopped postpartum bleeding in 73% of women within 20 minutes. 2
Making brain electrodes inspired by Japanese art For decades, scientists have been developing, testing, and implanting brain electrodes

These devices are literally inserted into people’s brains, so while they can help us understand brain activity and treat various neurological disorders, it’s not totally surprising that they can also cause a bit of damage
Xiao Yang, 34, is working on ultra-small electrodes, which she hopes will have less of an impact on surrounding brain tissue
Her electrodes are flexible, too—in fact, they look a lot like actual neurons
Yang is also creating sheets of electrodes to study brain cells in the lab
Inspired by kirigami—the traditional Japanese art of cutting paper to form three-dimensional shapes—she’s created a sheet of electrodes with a honeycombed structure shaped like a spiral basket
And she’s already using it to study brain cells. 3
Developing an all-new treatment for baby KJ In 2024, Kyle “KJ” Muldoon Jr. was born with a rare and potentially fatal genetic disorder
Sarah Grandinette was a member of a team that developed an entirely new, personalized treatment for him—a gene-editing therapy essentially designed to correct a genetic misspelling
Grandinette, who is now 26, created cells with KJ’s genetic variant and used them to screen gene-editing approaches; then she tested potential medicines in mice and monkeys
KJ ultimately got his first dose of the resulting treatment when he was about seven months old
He responded well and was eventually discharged from hospital
Reversing the aging process to treat eye disease The buzziest tech in longevity right now centers on reprogramming—attempts to rewind the age of cells by resetting them to a more embryonic-like state
In a study published in 2020, Yuancheng (Ryan) Lu (now 34) and his colleagues showed that a reprogramming therapy reversed vision loss in aged, blind mice
Now an almost identical version of that therapy is being tested in people with eye disease
Life Biosciences, the company developing the drug, dosed its first volunteer in June. 5

Once he had those blueprints, he printed them out as strands of DNA
In experiments, he found that those AI-designed viruses could create new copies of themselves, burst out of bacterial cells, and infect other nearby bacteria
Viruses aren’t alive, but King, 27, hopes that AI-designed life forms might one day be used to make drugs or soak up pollution

title: How anti-bribery laws apply to Trump’s promise of $5,000 payments if Republicans keep control of Congress
url:
<title>How anti-bribery laws apply to Trump’s promise of $5,000 payments if Republicans keep control of Congress</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759374/original/file-20260911-50-3skz6w.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=43%2C0%2C4233%2C2822&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">President Donald Trump speaks at the RNC midterm convention in Dallas on Sept. 9, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Election2026Republicans/28edb16b54864df889e79080c8f43c6c/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=President%20Trump&amp;currentItemNo=85&amp;startingItemNo=750&amp;sourceLocation=Search">Eric Lee/Pool photo via AP</a></span></figcaption></figure><p><a href="https://www.houstonpublicmedia.org/articles/news/politics/election-2026/2026/09/10/561450/trump-promises-5000-dividend-in-convention-speech-but-only-if-republicans-win/">In his keynote address</a> to the Republican midterm convention on Sept. 9, 2026, <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/10/trump-dividend-midterms-gop.html">President Donald Trump promised</a> that if Republicans retain control of Congress in November, he <a href="https://time.com/article/2026/09/10/trump-dividend-five-thousand-dollars-midterms-republican-convention/">would authorize a US$5,000 payment to every American adult</a>. </p>

<p>Trump’s offer seems to run afoul of federal laws, which make it <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/597">a crime to pay for votes</a>.</p>

<p>After Trump’s speech, <a href="https://x.com/samstein/status/2097870389489594746">political commentator Sam Stein posted</a> on X: “trump openly bribing people to vote for republicans. $5k per person if republicans hold the house and the senate?” </p>

<p>Stein was not alone in referencing bribery. Lisa Gilbert, co-president of Public Citizen, a consumer advocacy group, <a href="https://www.citizen.org/news/trumps-desperate-attempt-to-bribe-voters-ahead-of-election-is-a-new-low/">issued the following statement after Trump’s speech</a>: “Trump knows he can’t do this, and yet he’s attempting to bribe voters with the false promise of cash to help his party win an election.”</p>

<p>But as a <a href="https://press.umich.edu/Books/T/The-Rhetoric-of-Law">scholar of political and legal rhetoric</a>, I think it’s worth further examining what the president said and whether his promise violated any law.</p>

<h2>An American tradition</h2>

<p>Paying voters to support a particular candidate, or promising government jobs in exchange for votes, <a href="https://live-sas-www-history.pantheon.sas.upenn.edu/publications/2016/mary-frances-berry">has a long history</a> in the United States. <a href="https://billofrightsinstitute.org/essays/william-boss-tweed-and-political-machines/">It was a staple</a> of <a href="https://politicaldictionary.com/words/machine-politics/">machine politics</a> in big cities starting in the late 19th century. </p>

<p>The political scholar <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055408080106">Simeon Nichter argues</a> that it would be better to describe these practices as examples of “turnout buying.” <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055408080106">He notes</a> that “observers in various U.S. cities have complained that some politicians use ‘street money’ – small, unreported cash payments ostensibly used for legal get-out-the-vote efforts such as canvassing and transporting voters – as direct payments for turnout.”</p>

<p>What Nichter describes has made a comeback in our era.</p>

<p>Recall <a href="https://abc7news.com/story/elon-musk-broke-law-promising-voters-1-million-payouts-wisconsin-board-says/19515645/">Elon Musk’s effort to ensure a Republican victory</a> in a 2025 state Supreme Court election in Wisconsin. He spent millions in that effort and, as <a href="https://www.ap.org/news-highlights/elections/2026/elon-musk-likely-broke-the-law-by-promising-voters-1-million-payouts-wisconsin-board-says/">The Associated Press reported</a>, offered “$1 million to people who voted in the Supreme Court election” to encourage them to vote.</p>

<p>In July 2026, the Wisconsin Elections Commission <a href="https://apnews.com/article/elon-musk-wisconsin-election-million-dollar-checks-2900f27acc373c9f1661a934f00c0c3d">found enough evidence to refer</a> citizen complaints about Musk’s behavior to a district attorney, “which can choose,” as the AP notes, “to bring criminal charges over violating the state law against election bribery.” </p>

<p>A month later, a state prosecutor said he could <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/minnesota/news/elon-musk-wont-face-election-bribery-charges-in-wisconsin-state-prosecutor-says/">not prove Musk’s guilt beyond a reasonable doubt</a> and would not bring charges.</p>

<h2>Federal law</h2>

<p>Because state and federal laws differ, we can’t extrapolate from the Wisconsin decision to Trump’s $5,000 promise.</p>

<p>Two provisions of federal law relating to vote buying <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/597">were adopted by Congress</a> and became law in 1948. Both treated that practice as a form of election interference.</p>

<p>The first <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/597">reads as follows</a>: “Whoever makes or offers to make an expenditure to any person, either to vote or withhold his vote, or to vote for or against any candidate; and whoever solicits, accepts, or receives any such expenditure in consideration of his vote or the withholding of his vote; Shall be fined under this title or imprisoned … or both.”</p>

<p>The second <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/600">prohibits offering government benefits</a> “to any person as consideration, favor, or reward for any political activity or for the support of or opposition to any candidate or any political party in connection with any … election to any political office.”</p>

<p>Both provisions focus on the use of money or the promise of benefits to get individuals to vote in a particular way.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759375/original/file-20260911-70-b816kw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man in suit and tie shakes hands with women dress in red and white." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759375/original/file-20260911-70-b816kw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759375/original/file-20260911-70-b816kw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759375/original/file-20260911-70-b816kw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759375/original/file-20260911-70-b816kw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759375/original/file-20260911-70-b816kw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759375/original/file-20260911-70-b816kw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759375/original/file-20260911-70-b816kw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">President Trump arrives at the Republican convention in Dallas on Sept. 9, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Election2026Republicans/009ed2b88d3348e7a06ee52810941f9e/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=President%20Trump&amp;currentItemNo=90&amp;startingItemNo=850&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>But Trump did not make his offer to any particular voter or set of voters. And, unlike Musk, he was acting as a public figure. The president’s promise was directed to all voters, not just to those who vote Republican.</p>

<p>John Day, a former federal prosecutor, compared Trump’s “dividend” to <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/10/us/politics/trump-dividend-5000-check.html">a pledge to deliver a tax break</a>. “A promise to lower taxes also gives voters a financial reason to support a candidate, but that does not, by itself, make the promise a bribe,” Day told The New York Times.</p>

<h2>Supreme Court precedent</h2>

<p>In 1982, in Brown v. Hartlage, the Supreme Court <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/456/45/">weighed in on the legality of political figures</a> promising financial benefits to voters. It found nothing wrong with the practice so long as the benefit was not offered as a quid pro quo to a particular voter.</p>

<p>Writing for a unanimous court, Justice William Brennan said that a political candidate “no less than any other person, has a First Amendment right to engage in the discussion of public issues and vigorously and tirelessly to advocate his own election and the election of other candidates.” </p>

<p>In his view, that right includes making statements about financial gains voters might receive if a candidate or a party wins an election, as long as they were “made openly and were subject to the criticism of his political opponent and to the scrutiny of the voters.” Such statements, Brennan added, were different from “corrupting private agreements and solicitations historically recognized as unprotected by the First Amendment.”</p>

<p>The Hartlage decision remains the applicable precedent today.</p>

<p>A year after the court’s decision, however, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1086/scer.2.1147126">legal scholars Peter Aranson and Kenneth Shepsle argued</a> that the Supreme Court decision countered several lower court decisions that had treated promises of the kind the high court approved “as analogous to bribes, which would turn the citizenry’s attention away from ‘proper’ public policy issues.”</p>

<p>Trump may view the question of whether Republicans retain control of Congress as just such an issue.</p>

<h2>Beyond legality</h2>

<p>Whatever Trump’s view, <a href="https://www.aei.org/commentary/the-transactional-trap/">commentators have observed</a> that in Trump’s world, relationships are transactional. It is the deal that counts, not the values it promotes or undermines. So, the importance of Trump’s cash offer goes beyond the legal question of whether it is bribery, vote buying or a legitimate political promise. </p>

<p>It’s worth focusing attention on the virtues and vices of the transactional approach to politics, what it does to the character of U.S. political life and to the way Americans see the world.</p>

<p>One of Trump’s critics, the <a href="https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2025/03/political-enemy-retribution-efforts/682095/">former presidential speechwriter Peter Wehner</a>, describes what he calls “the great civic danger posed by Donald Trump” this way: “that the habits of his heart become the habits of our hearts: that his code of conduct becomes ours.”</p>

<p>Whether or not he is right, Wehner points Americans to a domain beyond law as the right place to assess the president’s promise of a “<a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/6081944-trump-dividend-pledge-backlash/">Trump Dividend</a>.”</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291722/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
<p class="fine-print"><em><span>Austin Sarat does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.</span></em></p></content>

title: Here’s how teachers and parents can collaborate and help Michigan’s 1.4M students succeed

<title>Here’s how teachers and parents can collaborate and help Michigan’s 1.4M students succeed</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754711/original/file-20260818-50-49qtqj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1697%2C5821%2C3881&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Family engagement can help students regularly attend classes, according to researchers. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/home/search?query=michigan%20students%20&amp;mediaType=photo">Paul Sancya/AP</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>About <a href="https://www.mischooldata.org/student-enrollment-counts-report/">1.4 million Michigan students</a> returned to the state’s K-12 public school classrooms this fall. </p>

<p>One of the most powerful influences on how these students will perform exists outside the classroom: the quality of the partnerships that schools and families establish with each other. </p>

<p>Establishing these partnerships may be easier than it sounds. Throughout more than four decades as an educator and <a href="https://education.msu.edu/people/e/edwards-patricia">researcher studying literacy and family engagement</a>, I have learned that most families deeply care about their children’s education and want to work with teachers toward the best possible outcomes.</p>

<h2>Family engagement helps students achieve</h2>

<p>This message is especially timely in Michigan. Many students continue to experience challenges in reading following the COVID-19 pandemic. Only <a href="https://www.mischooldata.org/grades-3-8-state-testing-includes-psat-data-performance/">39% of Michigan third graders</a> scored proficient or advanced in English language arts on the M-STEP, an annual state exam, in the 2024-25 school year.</p>

<p>In 2024, Michigan students scored below the national average in reading on the <a href="https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/">National Assessment of Educational Progress</a>. Michigan fourth graders <a href="https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/profiles/stateprofile/overview/mi?cti=PgTab_Findings&amp;sub=MAT&amp;chort=1&amp;year=2024R3&amp;st=MN&amp;sfj=NP&amp;sj=MI&amp;fs=Grade">averaged 209</a>, five points below the national average, while eighth graders averaged 255, compared with 257 nationally.</p>

<p>Although standardized test scores <a href="https://www.nea.org/student-success/standardized-testing-student-assessment">do not fully capture the breadth of students’ knowledge</a>, abilities or potential, they can provide <a href="https://nces.ed.gov/">one useful indicator</a> of how well students are developing literacy skills. </p>

<p><a href="https://bealearninghero.org/">National</a> <a href="https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA1108-8.html">studies</a> also demonstrate that families want to play active roles in their children’s education. They show, too, that many parents seek clearer communication and more meaningful opportunities to collaborate with educators. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Shelves filled with books inside a school library" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757927/original/file-20260904-60-jro6n8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757927/original/file-20260904-60-jro6n8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757927/original/file-20260904-60-jro6n8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757927/original/file-20260904-60-jro6n8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757927/original/file-20260904-60-jro6n8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757927/original/file-20260904-60-jro6n8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757927/original/file-20260904-60-jro6n8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Michigan students’ low literacy rates point to a need for more support.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/new-reading-space-is-seen-after-the-renovation-by-macys-and-news-photo/1649095008?adppopup=true">Aaron J. Thornton/Getty Images for Macy's Inc.</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In my assessment, one of the most encouraging developments in <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/1361332052000341006">family engagement research</a> over the past two decades has been the growing recognition among researchers, educators and schools that parents are not simply volunteers who occasionally assist schools. They are co-educators whose knowledge, cultural wealth and lived experiences enrich children’s educational opportunities. </p>

<p>This understanding reflects <a href="https://www.ed.gov/sites/ed/files/documents/family-community/partners-education.pdf">a broader movement</a> toward educational equity and shared responsibility for student success.</p>

<h2>Parents are partners in education</h2>

<p>Families may be invited to attend conferences, literacy nights or workshops, but they are not always invited to share their knowledge or participate as equal partners in decisions about their children’s learning. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Woman stand behind boy sitting at desk." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756634/original/file-20260827-50-7oznu7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756634/original/file-20260827-50-7oznu7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756634/original/file-20260827-50-7oznu7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756634/original/file-20260827-50-7oznu7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756634/original/file-20260827-50-7oznu7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756634/original/file-20260827-50-7oznu7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756634/original/file-20260827-50-7oznu7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

              <span class="caption">Families and educators who work together can help students develop stronger literacy skills.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/home/search?query=back%20to%20school%20michigan&amp;mediaType=photo">Paul Sancya/AP Photo</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In my experience, families may feel that educators do not understand their cultural and linguistic practices. They may notice that communication flows primarily from school to home rather than in both directions, or that their knowledge of their own children is undervalued.</p>

<p>For families whose previous encounters with schools have involved judgment, exclusion or racism, or educators focusing on perceived shortcomings rather than recognizing families’ strengths, an invitation to participate does not automatically create understanding.</p>

<p>Some of my most formative lessons came during my early work with African American families in Louisiana. I began spending time with parents and listening carefully to what they understood schools were asking them to do at home. </p>

<p>Teachers frequently encouraged parents to “read to your child,” without explaining what meaningful reading might look like. </p>

<p>Some parents were uncertain about teachers’ expectations or viewed reading primarily as getting the words right. These experiences helped inspire <a href="https://www.google.com/books/edition/Parents_as_Partners_in_Reading/u4p7PQAACAAJ?hl=en">Parents as Partners in Reading</a>, a program I designed to help families support children’s literacy through interactive read-alouds that encourage conversation and making connections between books and children’s everyday lives. </p>

<p>In Louisiana, I showed rather than simply told them how they might make reading with their children more interactive and enjoyable. I modeled how to sit comfortably with a child, let the child hold the book and turn the pages, vary their voices, pause to ask questions, talk together about the pictures and follow the child’s interests and reactions. </p>

<p>Rather than prescribing a single “right” way to read together, these interactions gave parents opportunities to try different approaches, ask questions and discover what worked best for them and their children.</p>

<p>Parents then practiced these approaches with one another before using them. As their confidence increased, the interactions began to flow more naturally: Parents relied less on the strategies I had modeled and became more comfortable following their children’s lead, responding to their questions and comments and allowing conversations about the story to develop spontaneously. </p>

              <span class="caption">Educators can learn from families about what their children’s interests and strengths are.</span>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Talking to families with empathy</h2>

<p>I’ve watched educators transform their relationships with families once they begin viewing parents through their strengths rather than perceived flaws. Families know dimensions of their children that may never be visible during the school day: the child who loves to tell stories at the dinner table, or the child who is fascinated by cars or animals.</p>

<p>When educators listen to those stories, they gain information that can change how they understand and teach a child. Family engagement must also mean creating opportunities for educators to learn from families.</p>

<p>Instead of asking why families are not involved, they begin asking <a href="https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED474521">how schools can become more welcoming</a>, more responsive and more collaborative. That shift in perspective often changes the entire culture of a school.</p>

<p>Here are a few ways educators can build relationships with families and vice versa:</p>

<p><strong>Build relationships before you need them</strong></p>

<p>Teachers shouldn’t wait until there is a problem to reach out to families. Relationships are strongest when schools communicate with families before challenges arise. </p>

<p>A welcoming phone call, a quick note celebrating something a child did well, an invitation to visit the classroom, or simply taking time to learn about a child’s interests can go a long way. </p>

<p>Parents can make a point of introducing themselves to their child’s teacher early in the school year. Parents might share something the teacher would find helpful to know about their child – what excites them, what they enjoy reading or doing at home, or what helps them feel confident as learners. </p>

<p>These early exchanges also communicate an important message: “I know my child in ways that can help you teach them, and I want us to work together.” </p>

<p><strong>Make communication a conversation</strong></p>

<p>Families should hear from educators, but educators also need to hear from families. Communication is most meaningful when educators listen as much as they inform. </p>

<p>Educators can ask parents and caregivers: What are your hopes for your child this year? What should I know about your child that will help me be a better teacher? How does your child learn best? What is the easiest way for us to stay in touch?</p>

<p>Parents can ask teachers: “What are you noticing about my child as a reader and learner?” and “What are some things we can do at home that would reinforce what you are teaching at school?” </p>

<p><strong>Bring empathy to difficult conversations</strong></p>

<p>At some point, educators may need to talk with families about academic, behavioral or attendance concerns. Teachers can begin by sharing what the child does well and listening to what the family is seeing at home. Then invite their insights and perspectives: “Here is what I’m noticing. What are you seeing, and how can we work together?” This small shift – from presenting families with a problem to inviting them into a conversation – can transform a potentially difficult exchange into an opportunity for genuine partnership.</p>

<p>Families can listen carefully when teachers raise concerns and ask questions to better understand what the teacher is observing about their child. They can also share what they notice about their child at home, since children may demonstrate different strengths, behaviors and abilities in different settings. </p>

<p>Together, families and teachers can identify strategies to try at home and at school to address the concern and agree on a time to reconnect and discuss the child’s progress.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/287763/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
