title: 25 years after 9/11, the GOP has never been more anti-Muslim
excerpt: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Rudy Giuliani arrive ahead of the 25th anniversary commemoration ceremony at the National 9/11 Memorial and Museum in Man
body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Rudy Giuliani arrive ahead of the 25th anniversary commemoration ceremony at the National 9/11 Memorial and Museum in Manhattan on September 11, 2026. | Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in  Today, Explained,  a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
Hi readers — today marks 25 years since 9/11
In New York City, Washington, and Pennsylvania, survivors, families, and politicians are gathering to grieve and commemorate the attacks

Today, we wanted to focus on one small part of the story in New York City, where former Mayor Rudy Giuliani singled out Mayor Zohran Mamdani , who is Muslim, with an Islamophobic screed about Mamdani’s participation in memorial ceremonies

Giuliani’s rant, to be clear, is not really news in its own right; 25 years on, he’s less “America’s mayor” than he is the twice – disbarred , disgraced former lawyer of President Donald Trump. (And Mamdani did attend the event, even shaking hands with Giuliani.) But Giuliani’s remarks are, unfortunately, emblematic of a disturbing trend in Republican politics, where open, aggressive Islamophobia is on the rise — 25 years after a particularly ugly brand of it emerged in response to 9/11
One major difference between then and now? In 2001, many politicians tried to tamp it down rather than inflame it

As Nathan Lean, an assistant teaching professor at North Carolina State University and author of the book The Islamophobia Industry , explained to my colleague Christian Paz last month : “Islamophobia has passed the dinner table test
You can say things about Muslims with basic impunity today

And it’s institutionalized in the way that prejudice that targets other marginalized communities is not.” The GOP is running on Islamophobia in 2026 The 2026 midterm elections have provided a particularly clear showcase for the right’s Islamophobic turn.  On Thursday, at the second and final night of the GOP’s unusual midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, Sen
Ted Cruz (R-TX) told attendees that “communism” and “Islamism” were allying against Republicans. “They share the same enemies,” he said. “They hate Christians

They hate the Constitution, and they hate America.”  At another point in Cruz’s speech, attendees screamed “he should be shot” as Cruz name-checked Mamdani, Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (who is Muslim, and who Cruz said “says he has an obligation to Sharia Law”), and Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico.  As Christian reports , Michigan and especially Texas have both been on the front lines of rising Islamophobia.  Michigan has a large Muslim population in cities like Dearborn and Hamtramck, and El-Sayed has drawn particular vitriol; Rep

Nancy Mace (R-SC) wrote last month that “Every single Muslim holding public office in America is a Trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic.”  And in Texas, as the New York Times reported at length last month , Islamophobia has become a matter of policy as well as rhetoric from Republican Gov

Greg Abbott and other politicians in the state.  El-Sayed, in Michigan, has described the attacks as an attempt to distract voters from other issues. “They’re going to point at me, they’re going to point at my name, like, ‘Wow, he’s different,’” he said last month . “My name is not raising your gas prices
My name is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.” Without much else to run on , though, Republicans seem to have decided they’re all-in on Islamophobia

On Vox’s Unexplainable podcast, the Switched on Pop team looks at how our brains can figure out a song just from its first few seconds, how it can influence our perception, and what we’re losing as recent hits begin to move away from intros.  Before you go… Did you know… that young readers tend to drop off around age 9 , even if they’re prolific readers before that? Publishers aren’t exactly sure why — but they’re hoping a new approach to “middle-grade books” could help reverse some of the decline.  Today’s trivia: Which country voted against restarting membership talks with the European Union this year? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in Monday’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the age of the world’s oldest-known oven
In 2009, archaeologists discovered an ancient oven in the Czech Republic that dated back to 29,000 BC and was used to roast woolly mammoths, among other things.

title: The one thing you can do to help a whole lot of animals, explained in 4 charts
excerpt: Many people, when they learn about the horrors of factory farming , become vegetarian or vegan
body: Many people, when they learn about the horrors of factory farming , become vegetarian or vegan
I’m one of those people, and it stuck — I haven’t eaten meat in 20 years
But new research highlights how ditching meat isn’t the only option to help animals on factory farms

There’s actually one thing that’s almost as effective and probably way easier for most people: eating fewer small animals.  The number of animals who suffer to produce food products — and how much they suffer — varies widely
Bigger animals, like cattle raised for beef, are raised in lower numbers and aren’t treated as terribly as smaller animals, like farmed fish and chickens
And because fish and chickens are so small, far more of them must be farmed to produce the same amount of meat as large animals

A family sitting down for a steak dinner, for example, will probably consume about half a percent of one cow, while a family eating a rotisserie chicken might eat the whole bird.  Animal advocates call it the “small body problem,” and it’s the subject of a new analysis published by Chris Bryant , an honorary research associate at the University of Bath in the UK, and Faunalytics , an animal welfare research group

The researchers wanted to answer a simple but consequential question: How much animal suffering is embedded in each bite of meat we eat or egg we consume?  “We are somewhat used to seeing, especially from the climate movement, data and other kinds of tools that help us think about the carbon footprint of the choices that we make, and we think that’s really important,” Allison Troy, Faunalytics’ research director, told me. “But we felt like there was a gap in terms of thinking about more of a ‘suffering footprint’ when it comes to choosing to purchase animal products.” This gives us a new way to think about how we eat, and how it affects the animals trapped in factory farms

If you don’t want to go fully plant-based, what about cutting back — specifically — on meat from small animals? Unpacking the small body problem To quantify the “suffering footprint” of everyday animal products consumers eat, the researchers analyzed data from the US Department of Agriculture, the United Nations, and other sources to determine how much edible meat — or eggs or milk — each type of farmed animal produces throughout a typical lifespan on a farm
They also incorporated indirect sources of animal suffering in their calculations
For example, some farmed fish species are fed other fish, and these “feeder” fish were factored into the data

Then the researchers crunched the numbers to figure out two things: how many days of animal suffering are embedded in a pound of various animal products, and how many animal lives are slaughtered per pound for those products
The analysis found that the vast majority of animal suffering from our diets comes from one tiny animal: shrimp
That means that a single bite of your shrimp scampi is far more harmful than devouring an entire burger
But seafood doesn’t account for a large portion of most Americans’ diets , and many of us eat none at all
When seafood is removed from the data, cutting back on poultry products — chicken meat, turkey meat, and eggs — is the most effective way to limit the amount of suffering caused by one’s diet

This enormous disparity in poultry versus other categories “is driven by the fact that those are smaller-bodied animals — it just takes a larger number of animals to produce consumable products for people,” Troy said. “And I don’t think that that’s often a way that people think about animal products when they’re making these decisions.”  Chickens and turkeys also tend to be treated worse than cattle and pigs

Chickens raised for meat, for example, have been bred to grow so fast , and so big, that many have difficulty standing and walking, while half of hens raised for eggs in the US are confined in small cages for their entire lives.  That doesn’t mean pigs and cattle have it easy — far from it
Pork producers, for example, typically castrate and teeth-clip piglets without pain relief, and the pigs spend their lives indoors
Female breeding pigs , like caged hens, are confined in tiny cages
And beef cattle are branded and dehorned , often without pain relief, and spend their final months in feedlots

But because these animals are so much bigger, each produces a lot more meat than smaller animals.  In other words, their suffering is spread out across many more bites of bacon or burgers.  Going beyond the numbers The report wasn’t peer-reviewed, and I reached out to Trevor Woolley — an assistant professor of agricultural and applied economics at the University of Wisconsin-Madison — for his thoughts

Woolley told me over email that it’s “important to recognize that the numbers that are included in their equation are estimates,” and that “the exact numbers should not be taken as precise, but in the right ballpark.” How should I think about eggs?  It might come as a surprise that eating fewer eggs is one of the best actions you can take to help animals, considering it doesn’t require killing animals

Still, egg-laying hens tend to have poor welfare; about half of them in the US are in tiny cages where they can’t flap their wings for their entire lives, and the tips of their beaks are seared off without pain relief
Once their productivity wanes — at about 1.5 years of age — they’re slaughtered for meat

Eating fewer eggs , and getting “pasture-raised” eggs when you do buy them, can help (if you’re looking for information on what the various buzzwords on egg cartons actually mean, we’ve got you covered ). “Comparing animal products in terms of lives and (especially) days broadly makes sense,” Woolley added. “‘Days’ is a really nice metric because farm animal species have such drastically different lifespans on the farm.” There is, however, one major limitation to the research: it doesn’t factor in the severity of suffering that different animals experience. “We made a choice methodologically to define ‘animal suffering’ as days of life [on a farm],” Troy said. “And I think that that’s a useful, albeit simple, metric
But it is not the only one.” For example, on a day-to-day basis, dairy cows don’t seem to have it as bad as an egg-laying hen in a cage
But dairy cows tend to be farmed for twice as many years as hens

Does that suffering over many years compound in a way that, if we could fully understand it, would change the calculation? This analysis can’t answer nuanced questions like that, though other animal welfare researchers are working to provide a more comprehensive picture. “If you can stand to think about it long enough, the problem becomes paralyzing,” my colleague Marina Bolotnikova has written about factory farming. “Tens of billions of land animals are slaughtered every year; hundreds of millions every day; thousands in the time it takes to read this sentence
The number grows by billions more every year, into multiples that feel as abysmal as they are mind-numbing.” It’s enough to cause a lot of people to tune out and ignore the problem altogether
But shrinking these figures down to the impact our own diets have on animals is much more manageable
We can think smaller and maybe, while we’re at it, eat fewer small animals.

title: Trump keeps telling voters he doesn’t care much about affordability
excerpt: President Donald Trump during the first day of the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on September 9, 2026. | Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images If the mi
body: President Donald Trump during the first day of the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on September 9, 2026. | Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images If the midterms were a referendum on whether trans athletes should be barred from women’s sports, or the White House ballroom should be gorgeously renovated , or God should be identified as “nonbinary,” then Republicans would have a clear and confident closing message
Key takeaways The cost of living is midterm voters’ top issue
The war in Iran has led to the first decline in real wages since 2023
Trump could bring gas prices down before Election Day by seeking a ceasefire with Iran, but he’s choosing to prioritize military victory
The president is also escalating trade wars, despite their impact on consumer prices
Unfortunately for the GOP, voters are less concerned with the Christian deity’s preferred pronouns than with their own cost of living

Which is understandable: Diesel fuel prices just hit a record high, mortgage rates are climbing , and groceries keep getting more expensive.  Due partly to these trends, Republicans are poorly positioned to win an argument about inflation — and are only growing more so, as Election Day nears
This was apparent before President Donald Trump convened the first-ever Republican midterm convention in Dallas this week
But the festivities underscored the GOP’s predicament and the many ways that Trump is personally exacerbating it
Many Republican speakers did address the subject of affordability in Dallas
And the party’s broad narrative is straightforward enough: Democrats created the cost-of-living crisis, Republicans alleviated it by cutting your taxes
Americans might still disdain President Joe Biden’s economic management
Yet they’re far more likely to blame high prices on the current president than the previous one, according to polls.  And not without reason
After all, it was Trump — not Biden — who engineered an oil shock and global trade war
Tellingly, on Wednesday night, all four battleground state Senate candidates — Ken Paxton, Jon Husted, Michael Whatley, and Mike Collins — made no mention of the Iran war or of Trump’s tariffs
If Republican frontliners are clear-eyed about their party’s liabilities, Trump seems largely indifferent to them
Historically, presidents have often made an effort to limit election-year price increases — and/or, to reduce the salience of their party’s worst issues
Yet Trump has been doing the very opposite.  In recent weeks, the president has escalated his conflict with Iran and his trade war with US allies , driving up Americans’ costs in the process
And he’s been remarkably frank about his refusal to prioritize affordability
In his remarks to the convention Wednesday, Trump impersonated a disaffected constituent, saying, “You know, I wish you didn’t do the war in Iran

Gasoline’s up, ba ba ba” — before explaining to this critic that preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon took precedence over their energy costs.  Republicans may still weather a midterm backlash
The party remains narrowly favored to retain the Senate, while gerrymandered maps should limit its losses in the House
But if this year’s “blue wave” proves less than tidal, it will be in spite of Trump’s efforts, not because of them

The GOP’s very simple problem The Republican Party’s fundamental problem is simple: Voters’ top concern is the cost of living — and American purchasing power has fallen sharply in 2026, as a direct result of the president’s policies
In virtually every poll, a plurality of voters name “ inflation ,” “ the cost of living ,” or “ affordability ” as their most important issue
And they are not impressed with Trump’s record on that front

In a recent Ipsos survey, 74 percent of respondents said that their cost of living is “off on the wrong track.” Meanwhile, in Nate Silver’s poll tracker , more than 70 percent of Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of inflation, up from just 41 percent when he took office
Silver Bulletin " /> During his first year in office, Trump could have reasonably argued that voters were giving him a bad rap on the economy
After all, real wages — how much Americans earn per hour, adjusted for inflation — actually rose in 2025, even as disapproval of the president’s economic record surged

But in February 2026, Trump brought nearly three years of real wage growth to a screeching halt: By launching a war with Iran — and thus, triggering its closure of the Strait of Hormuz — Trump triggered the first sustained decline in Americans’ purchasing power since 2022

View Link According to an estimate from Brown’s Watson School, the Iran war has cost the average US household more than $780 through elevated energy prices.  Politically, this seems to have made a real difference
At the beginning of March, Trump’s net approval rating on inflation was -28, according to Nate Silver’s polling average; as of this writing, it is -45.9
At this point, there may be little Trump can do to gain broad public trust on the cost of living
But political science research suggests that economic trends in the runup to Election Day can shift votes at the margin
And precisely because this year’s price spike is largely self-inflicted, Trump has an unusual amount of power to increase affordability before Americans head to the polls
All he’d need to do is reach a ceasefire (or, ideally, peace deal) with Iran
We know Trump could bring down energy costs by pursuing peace because he already has

Throughout 2026, oil prices have consistently fallen whenever the US-Iran war has cooled off  — and risen whenever it has intensified.  When Trump signaled an imminent ceasefire deal in early June , the price of an oil barrel swiftly fell, dropping below $75
Once that ceasefire broke down early the next month, oil prices resumed their climb, until Trump paused US strikes on July 25

title: Powering AI is an architecture problem
excerpt: On July 22, 2026, a transmission line fault in Ashburn, Virginia—the heart of the world’s largest data center cluster—knocked more than 3 gigawatts of loa
body: On July 22, 2026, a transmission line fault in Ashburn, Virginia—the heart of the world’s largest data center cluster—knocked more than 3 gigawatts of load off the grid in seconds
Two years earlier, a single failed surge arrester dropped roughly 60 Virginia facilities and 1,500 megawatts at once
No one could anticipate so much uniform load responding to grid faults the same way, at the same time
The AI power debate is mostly about generation: more turbines, more solar, more transmission
But the outages in Virginia weren’t supply failures; they were architecture failures
And a giant wave of interconnections is arriving on that same architecture, putting grid reliability at risk
Asking more from the grid The grid was built around predictable loads: steel mills, refineries, and houses at dinnertime
Different load sizes, same process—drawing power smoothly, misbehaving occasionally, and recovering gracefully
But AI data centers don’t behave that way
An AI campus can swing 70% of its load in milliseconds during a training run, then trip offline just as fast at the first sign of trouble upstream to protect billions in compute
Together, at gigawatt scale, they’re a problem the grid has never solved—and the next wave of data center campuses is planned at exactly that scale
Where the old stack breaks The standard data center power stack hasn’t changed in decades
Medium-voltage power arrives, transformers step it down, low-voltage uninterruptible power supply (UPS) units condition it, and it reaches the racks
Push that design to AI scale, and it cracks in three places
First, the UPS sits deep inside the building, close to the racks
But its batteries are an undersized spare tire, designed to handle an outage for a few minutes, not to absorb load swings this fast and volatile around the clock
Second, the UPS spends most of its life in bypass
Legacy converters waste enough power that operators run in eco-mode: A static switch feeds the racks directly from the grid and nothing filters in either direction
The compute’s swings go out raw, and grid transients—sub-millisecond events that can damage or take down equipment—come in too fast for any switch to catch
Third, the protection logic was written when “large load” meant 50 megawatts
This protection logic can’t see the grid it is now a part of, so when trouble hits upstream, it does exactly the wrong thing: it drops out
In the 2024 Virginia event, most of the lost load traced to protection schemes that count voltage dips and disconnect on the third one —as designed, at the worst moment
It’s careful engineering the load has outgrown
Moving into the path The fix is three moves, made together
Move it up —from 480 volts to medium voltage (13.8 kilovolts and higher), the voltage large sites draw from the grid
Move it out —from the data hall to modular enclosures near the substation so the building holds only compute and the cooling that keeps it alive
Move it into the path —instead of a battery that watches and reacts, a system every electron runs through, all the time
There’s nothing to detect and nothing to switch because nothing was ever routed around it
In practice, they rewrite every line item downstream
Making the change When thousands of GPUs spin up together, the system absorbs the swing and hands the grid a flat load profile
When a disturbance hits, the equipment behind it never notices
A difficult neighbor becomes a predictable one
And when the utility needs help, it becomes a useful one
The utility certifies one medium-voltage box instead of untangling every transformer, UPS, chiller, pump, and switchgear lineup behind it
Engineers swap chip generations without a fresh interconnection study
Inside the fence, UPS rooms become compute or cooling space
Equipment that runs at medium voltage, sits outside, and stores its own energy can qualify for tax credits, and earn revenue in grid programs like peak shaving and demand response
Backup power stops being insurance and starts paying for itself
The architecture test In early 2026, we tested a full-scale system at the National Laboratory of the Rockies, a U.S
Department of Energy facility and the only place in the Western Hemisphere that can replicate real grid faults and AI-scale load swings concurrently in the same loop

title: This road map could help us decide whether to deploy solar geoengineering
excerpt: A San Francisco nonprofit has published a detailed road map of the experiments, studies, and infrastructure that it says would be needed to make informed decisi
body: A San Francisco nonprofit has published a detailed road map of the experiments, studies, and infrastructure that it says would be needed to make informed decisions about the use of solar geoengineering, MIT Technology Review can reveal

Scientists have now spent half a century exploring the possibility that we could counteract climate change by releasing reflective particles into the stratosphere, mimicking the cooling effects of volcanic eruptions.  But even after at least hundreds of studies on the concept, known as stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI), big gaps remain in the scientific understanding of how well it would work and what else it might do—and there has been no systematic plan for clearing up that uncertainty

Reflective, a research organization that funds studies on solar geoengineering, has today attempted to fill that gap with the release of its SAI Research Roadmap . “Our mission is to equip the world with the data and tools required for informed decision-making about sunlight reflection fast enough to matter,” says Dakota Gruener, the organization’s cofounder and chief executive. “Our sense is the world may need to make very consequential decisions on timelines far shorter than our research system is prepared for.” The hope is the exercise will guide scientific efforts and encourage philanthropies or government agencies to fund high-priority work and “responsibly accelerate research,” says Gruener

If all the work is done in a coordinated way, it would take about a decade and cost around $370 million—and if it’s not, it would require roughly 20 years and nearly $1.4 billion, the report estimates

While Gruener stresses that Reflective doesn’t advocate using this form of solar geoengineering, the report does make the case for conducting outdoor experiments, which would release successively larger amounts of sulfur dioxide (or materials that would convert into it) in the stratosphere to observe what happens

Since 2002, hundreds of academics have signed an open letter calling for a ban on outdoor experiments and an “international non-use agreement,” arguing that such a powerful technology could never be governed in a globally equitable way

And some signatories argue that more studies can never address one of the biggest questions about using solar geoengineering: Who gets to do it.   “The first-order questions, from my perspective, are not technical,” Aarti Gupta, co-initiator of the non-use initiative and professor of global environmental governance at Wageningen University in the Netherlands, told me in a recent on-stage interview .  “The core question is: Who would control a planet-altering technology like stratospheric aerosol injection? Who would develop it, and who would deploy it, and to what end? To serve what purposes, and whose purposes? Those questions are very fundamental, because this planet-altering technology will have winners and losers.” ‘Fast enough to matter’ Since Gruener incorporated Reflective in late 2023, the nonprofit has quickly become an important player in solar geoengineering research
It has now raised more than $20 million from a number of prominent charities and individuals , and it’s provided around $4 million to several dozen research groups

Reflective has also undertaken a handful of its own projects to promote research, including the development of an open-source solar geoengineering simulator and an online hub for collaborative research

Earlier this year, Reflective released its SAI Uncertainties database , which identified a long list of scientific unknowns and  engineering obstacles that would need to be addressed before even a small-scale solar geoengineering effort could move ahead. (I wrote about the specific scenario and the unknowns in this earlier piece .) Some of the biggest uncertainties involve what gas or particles would make the most sense to use and what would happen once they were released in the dry stratosphere

It’s not clear, for example, whether they’d spread out in a way that maximizes the reflectivity—or clump together and quickly fall out into the troposphere, the lowest layer of Earth’s atmosphere.  The road map builds upon the database, highlighting the path to addressing most of those questions.  The road map The initial phase in Reflective’s road map, labeled “foundational knowledge,” includes additional computer simulation studies and lab experiments designed to shed light on the potential impacts on different regions, ecosystems, and phenomena, including ocean circulation patterns, ice sheets, and crop yields.  The report also notes the need to begin developing more observational tools during this phase to improve understanding of the baseline conditions of the stratosphere—and, in turn, our ability to assess any effects from the eventual release of materials

This first stage would last two to three years and cost $30 million to $75 million, though some of the analysis and observational work would continue into subsequent phases.  The next stage would include using modified aircraft to release 10 metric tons of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere, four times over the course of two seasons
The full research stage could take four to eight years and cost $70 million to $150 million, the report says
The work during it may reduce uncertainty about the “cooling efficacy” of solar geoengineering, or how much the planet would cool per ton of sulfur released, by about 25%
The experiments during the next phase would step those levels up dramatically, releasing 25,000 tons of sulfur dioxide over the course of one season, at least once but possibly twice
That research stage, which includes other work as well, would last four to 11 years, run $270 million to $1.1 billion, and decrease efficacy uncertainty by around 66%, according to the road map
The final phase of research would be ongoing monitoring of full-scale solar geoengineering, if the world goes ahead with it

The goal would be to gather real-life data on the technology in action, update estimates of the effects in models, and spot any “unexpected or undesired consequences.” Gruener says that the road map is intended as a Version 1, meant to be “concrete enough for people to argue with.” But Reflective intends to update the plan as it receives additional reactions from researchers and other observers, and it will invite such feedback through a mechanism on the site

She also notes that there are firm “stage gates,” set up between the latter stages—in other words, research shouldn’t proceed to the next phase if the experiments suggest that the releases don’t have the hoped-for impact, show worrisome downsides, or fail to resolve crucial uncertainties. “Our road map has these gates precisely because there may be points where the answer is ‘You should stop,’” she says

Termination shock Most observers I spoke to about the report agree that these studies could reduce uncertainty about the effectiveness of solar geoengineering and our technical ability to carry it out.  But highlighting the scientific importance of outdoor experiments won’t necessarily make them any easier to move ahead with
Several earlier proposals to carry out such experiments, including Harvard’s SCoPEx and the UK-based SPICE project , were ultimately halted amid opposition from environmentalists or policymakers

In addition, not everyone agrees that experiments at those scales will get us to the point where we’re capable of making an “informed decision.”  Wil Burns, a research professor and legal scholar at American University and a signatory to the International Non-Use Agreement, fears that scientists won’t be able to understand the extent of the potential downsides, including impacts on the protective ozone layer and changes to regional precipitation patterns, until we’re carrying out full-fledged solar geoengineering. “The research would give you some answers,” he says. “I just don’t think it gives you answers that are that relevant

To get to those relevant answers, you have to deploy at scale—and I just don’t think that’s ever tenable.” That’s because, in his view, using the technology would violate principles of intergenerational equity: If the world continues emitting greenhouse gases, increased levels of solar geoengineering would merely mask the continued warming of the planet

Burns says that means future generations—people who had no say in its use—couldn’t turn it off without triggering a sudden surge of warming, known as termination shock .  “What that would do, in my mind, is put a sword of Damocles over future generations,” he says. “So even if you could, quote-unquote, ‘prove it works,’ I don’t think from an intergenerational perspective it would ever be tenable.” (Some researchers, however, have argued that the risks of termination shock are less likely than often assumed—and that solar geoengineering could be slowly dialed down over time.) ‘The right approach’ Ilan Gur, the former CEO of the Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA), the UK research department that funded 21 geoengineering research projects last year, applauds Reflective’s road map.  “Whether you’re a scientist or a policymaker or just a concerned citizen, our goal should be as quickly and efficiently as possible to answer the biggest questions scientifically that would tell us [whether] this is an approach that might work or that would never work,” he says. “We should all want to spend the effort and money to buy down that uncertainty, so my view is 100% the approach that Reflective is taking is the right one.” Sebastian Eastham, an associate professor in sustainable aviation at Imperial College London who is leading an ARIA-funded research project exploring another approach to engineered cooling, agrees that the outdoor experiments described in the Reflective road map can’t resolve all the unknowns

But he says the map helps begin a conversation about how to make decisions concerning the use of a tool with potential benefits and risks, in the face of escalating climate dangers. “Every hard decision that has ever been taken has been in the context of unresolved uncertainty,” he says. “That’s just the nature of things.” Eastham adds that it’s become essential to move beyond computer simulations to address some of the key questions, arguing that appropriately designed and executed outdoor experiments can teach us so much more than millions of hours of computational processing time “that it almost becomes irresponsible to say, ‘Well, there cannot be ever any experiment.’” The risk is “that we spin our wheels running the same computational simulations over and over and over again,” he says

That could prevent researchers from learning essential things about the effectiveness or the dangers of stratospheric aerosol injection.  Weighing the risks Gruener says the risks that solar geoengineering could exacerbate inequality need to be considered, but notes that unchecked warming also threatens to disproportionately harm developing regions
She also acknowledges that outdoor experiments won’t fully address the scientific unknowns but stresses that they can answer a lot—and carry little environmental risk

She notes that 10 tons of sulfur dioxide is less than 2% of the amount that the global aviation industry releases into the atmosphere each day. “Some people will be uncomfortable with any discussion of any outdoor experiment, but if we want decisions made on good science … then these are questions that an experiment will be necessary to address,” Gruener says

She fears that the rising dangers of climate change will put growing pressure on nations and other actors to move forward with solar geoengineering, even if no one has done the necessary research to reduce scientific uncertainty and sort out the technical challenges. “We don’t think the alternative is decisions not happening at all,” she says. “We think the alternative is decisions being made in a panic or on lack of evidence.”

title: The GOP midterms strategy is Trump and a prayer
excerpt: People hold signs on the first day of the 2026 Republican National Convention in Dallas. | Brandon Bell/Getty Images Welcome to The Midterms, Actually
body: People hold signs on the first day of the 2026 Republican National Convention in Dallas. | Brandon Bell/Getty Images Welcome to The Midterms, Actually
Every week I’ll be writing about two things: one big idea or trend I see forming across the 2026 primaries, and one thing I’m hearing from a voice on the ground
You can sign up here to get it in your inbox every week
One big idea: What are Republicans actually running on?  The first-of-its-kind Republican midterms convention began in the same vein as President Donald Trump’s second term: open grift

The president announced a pledge to give every American $5,000 if Republicans win the House and the Senate — part of what he’s calling a new dividend for American voters, and what some Democrats are calling an attempted bribe
Obviously, there are lots of questions about Trump’s announcement: Who will pay for the $1 trillion-plus dividend? Taxpayers
Could this even happen without congressional approval? Probably not
Why not just vote on it now, while Republicans control Congress? It would likely fail

But I think the pronouncement — and the GOP convention broadly — is best understood as a proxy for the Republican message in the midterm elections, not a policy roadmap for what Trump would do if Republicans maintained control of the House and Senate

So what can we actually glean from the GOP’s two-day bonanza in Dallas, and how does the message they were offering on that made-for-TV platform match up with the message they’ve delivered on the campaign trail? I took a close look at the convention speeches on Wednesday and Thursday, dug through our America, Actually reporting focusing on Republican voters and their candidates, and pulled together some trends that help explain the GOP strategy for defying the odds (and the polling) come Election Day. 1
Republicans are mostly in hiding One reason Trump’s midterm convention sticks out in this year’s landscape: It’s one of the rare places Republicans will campaign out loud
Congressional candidates, even in battleground House districts, have rarely held public events or town halls this year
And as Trump’s unpopularity has continued to grow, driven by rising gas prices and an unpopular war with Iran, it’s not like the GOP has responded by mounting a defense of its leader
They’ve mostly gone AWOL, a result of the electoral pickle the president has put them in

Trump is undoubtedly still the most powerful figure within the party, particularly among the Republican base, but Trump is also the biggest motivator for the Democratic base, and is increasingly off-putting to independent voters, who backed him in 2024

His approval has sunk to 33 percent in one recent Reuters/Ipsos poll, the lowest of his presidency , and that same poll found Democrats markedly more fired up for the midterms than Republicans — an enthusiasm gap that’s poison for the party in power

The independents who put him over the top have soured as the war drags on: a UMass poll found more than two-thirds disapprove of his handling of Iran nationally, and four in five say the war has driven up their gas and food prices
So when Trump tells voters at the GOP midterm convention to “pretend that he’s on the ballot” and turn out in November, I think his opponents listen with glee

Democrats are in the position they’re in because of a brewing electoral backlash to Trump — and the reason Republicans are so hard to find on the campaign trail is that they sense that same backlash is brewing, too
Check out what Ted Cruz said on The View this week: “The big open question is, do Republicans show up?” Cruz asked. “If we stay home, there’s a blue wave.” 2
Even Trump is on the defensive It’s rare to see Trump acknowledge any semblance of failure, but he came close during his speech during the convention’s first night

Trump was clearly on the defensive throughout his remarks: he sought to make the case for his (unpopular) tariff policy, he defended the (deeply unpopular) Iran war but without the usual bluster, and he acknowledged that gas prices may not fall until after Election Day
Last year, he predicted gas prices would soon hit $2 a gallon; this week he’s asking for still more patience after they hit a record $4.15 on Labor Day
From his speech: “You know, it happens to me all the time
Guys come up, ‘You know, I wish you didn’t do the war in Iran, gasoline’s up, ba, ba, ba.’ And I say, ‘Well, let me ask you…let me ask you one question
Can Iran have a nuclear weapon?’ ‘Absolutely not.’ ‘Well, then I’m right, then I win, okay?’”  But it’s worth remembering that “be patient” is a controversial message even among Republican voters

When our America, Actually team spent a day outside gas stations in Allentown this summer — deep in PA-7, one of the most contested House districts in the country ( watch the episode ) — we heard a clean split
There were some Republicans willing to eat the higher price in service of Trump’s war: “Yes, because our president is actually doing something about Iran

It’s something we need to do, and in the long run it’s gonna be better for everybody.” And there were other Republicans who voted for Trump and are furious: “I voted for him with his promises to the American people…and I think he’s let us down.” Another put the broken promise plainly: “I blame the president because he indicated to us he’s gonna drop all these costs
I know it can’t happen overnight, but when is it gonna happen? It’s outrageous.” The message now is to wait until after the election
A lot of the president’s own voters at the pump aren’t sure they can. 3
Notice the candidates who weren’t there Maybe the most revealing thing about Trump’s convention was the guest list, or more notably, the no-shows
MAGA celebrities who owe their careers to Trump packed the stage, but not a lot of the Republicans who are actually on the ballot in places they must win
Notable absences include candidates like John Sununu in New Hampshire and Susan Collins in Maine, and various congressional candidates from battleground races

And while their political calculus may be obvious — they want to avoid a Dallas-with-Trump photo op that ends up in a challenger’s attack ad — it reflects the “win by hiding” strategy that candidates not named Vivek Ramaswamy seem to be deploying

Here’s the play in a nutshell: keep enough distance from Trump to maintain credibility and independence, but rely on Trump to raise money, drive up Republican turnout, and savagely attack Democratic opponents

When conservative activist CJ Pearson came on our show , he insisted the GOP doesn’t have an electability problem at all — voters will see Democrats as too radical on topics like socialism and transgender women in sports, which came up repeatedly in the convention, and Republicans can still find ways to address affordability concerns. “These are 80/20 issues,” he said. ”And so I actually really like our odds here…we’re going to overperform

The House will be a dogfight, but I like our chances.” He even predicted this exact week, telling me the party would “see a change in his messaging and a reset at the midterm convention in Dallas,” after which “you’ll see those numbers start to change.” Whether Dallas actually delivered that reset — or just a $5,000 bribe and a defensive Trump — is, generously, an open question
And the attendance sheet suggests some of Pearson’s own party’s candidates aren’t waiting around to find out. 4
The JD Vance tightrope One person who doesn’t have the benefit of keeping distance from Trump is JD Vance, his vice president and the presumed GOP frontrunner for the 2028 presidential nomination

title: The interview Trump doesn’t want you to see
excerpt: Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico speaks at a campaign rally in Eagle Pass, Texas, on July 13, 2026. | Brandon Bell/Getty Images This story appeared in
body: Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico speaks at a campaign rally in Eagle Pass, Texas, on July 13, 2026. | Brandon Bell/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump’s FCC wants to keep a Democratic Senate candidate off the air.  What’s happening? On Wednesday, late-night host Jimmy Kimmel announced that his upcoming interview with James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas, would not air on TV.  Instead, he said , “due to circumstances beyond our comprehension,” it would be posted only on YouTube

According to Kimmel, Trump’s Federal Communications Commission “has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations, based on simple, traditional editorial decisions — guest bookings it would seem they don’t like.” Can Trump do that? It’s unclear — but he can at least make it painful enough for companies that they decide it’s not worth the headache
Kimmel said on Wednesday that his show’s decision was made “out of consideration for our local stations…who would have to deal with this nonsense” if they aired the interview

Late-night shows like Kimmel’s Jimmy Kimmel Live! have long been considered exempt from something called the equal-time rule, which requires broadcasters to give equal air time for candidates contending for the same office.  In January, however, the Trump administration said that late-night shows needed to comply with the rule; the next month, CBS declined to air an interview with Talarico on its late-night show, The Late Show with Stephen Colbert . (That interview was also posted to YouTube , where it’s since garnered about 9.5 million views.) What’s the context? This is not Kimmel’s first brush with Trump or the FCC

He was briefly suspended around this time last year after threats from Trump’s FCC chair, and Trump tried again to get him fired earlier this year , with less success.  Last month, ABC and its parent company, Disney, sued the FCC over its attempt to force a review of ABC’s broadcast licenses.  What’s the big picture? This kind of attack on the media is a familiar tactic from competitive authoritarian systems like Hungary, as my colleague Zack Beauchamp explained last year
Trump’s efforts to do the same in the US have often been clumsy or unsuccessful — but in this case, it seems to be working

And with that, it’s time to log off… Here’s a fun, strange story from Chicago: The city found a very big, very old boulder in the process of excavating to expand O’Hare Airport, and now it’s holding a contest to name the rock
You can read all about it (and find the link to suggest a name) here
Have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow!
